title: Musa's mother and sister
hookLine: a mother who trusted, a sister who followed along the bank (28:7–13)

cards: Pharaoh's household pulled a chest out of the river, with a baby inside. But someone put that chest in the water.
And someone else walked along the bank, watching it float away, keeping far enough back that no one noticed her. Two women at the start of Musa's life, one at each end of the danger.
The Qur'an doesn't name either of them. It tells you exactly what each one did.

teach.h: PUT HIM IN THE RIVER, AND DON'T FEAR.
teach.b: Surah al-Qasas, verse seven. Pharaoh is killing the boys of the Israelites.
Allah inspires Musa's mother: nurse him, and when you fear for him, put him in the river, and don't fear and don't grieve; We'll bring him back to you and make him a messenger.
The safest place for her son is the very thing a mother would keep him from: moving water. She does it.
Verse ten is honest about the cost: her heart became empty, and she nearly gave his secret away, if Allah hadn't steadied her heart. Then the sister. Verse eleven: the mother tells her, follow him.
In Arabic, qussihi: track him. She watches from a distance, and, the verse says, they didn't notice her. The chest reaches the palace.
The baby refuses every nurse they bring. And the sister steps forward at exactly the right moment: shall I show you a household who'll care for him and wish him well?

So Musa goes home, nursed by his own mother, now with Pharaoh's protection. Verse thirteen: so that she'd be comforted and not grieve, and know that Allah's promise is true. Here's a detail a scholar enjoys.
Qussihi comes from the root q-s-s, to follow tracks.

The same root gives qasas, stories, because telling a story is following events step by step. It's the name of this surah. The sister who followed the trail is inside the word for the whole book of stories.
The Hebrew Bible, in later chapters, names the two women Jochebed and Miriam. The Qur'an leaves them unnamed, and remembers every step.

how: Muslims retell the story of Musa's mother as a model of trust in Allah's promise, and his sister's quiet watching as a picture of family loyalty; the story is read in surah al-Qasas and surah Ta-Ha.

o: hide him, said to Musa's mother at the river
follow his tracks, said to Musa's sister
tell his story, the name of the surah itself

games.q: Musa's mother and sister — tap the pairs.

s: the Qur'an names Musa's mother and sister
it leaves them unnamed; the Hebrew Bible names them Jochebed and Miriam.
Musa ended up nursed by his own mother
he refused every other nurse, and his sister pointed the way home (28:12–13).
the Qur'an says his mother felt no fear
verse ten: her heart became empty, and Allah steadied it.

games.q: you're Musa's sister. the baby has reached the palace and refuses every nurse. what do you do?
o: run home and tell your mother.
offer to show them a household who will care for him.
games.why: she offers a household, without revealing who she is, and Musa is returned to his own mother (28:12–13).

practice: Bring to mind one person who's drifting a little out of reach right now: a teenager, a friend going through something, an elderly parent, a coworker who's gone quiet.
You can't carry them, but you can walk the bank, so picture what quiet watching would look like: noticing what they need before they ask. If you pray, you can pray for them by name.

wordCard.voice: Qussihi. Follow his tracks: Musa's mother trusted him to the river, and his sister tracked him along the bank, both unnamed, both remembered. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic, 28:11: follow his tracks, from q-s-s, the root of qasas, stories.

carryVoice: Your line: she followed along the bank. Quiet watching, from a distance, still counts. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Qur'an 20:38–40 (the chest on the river; the sister)
Exodus 2:1–10; Exodus 6:20; Numbers 26:59 (the Hebrew Bible names Jochebed and Miriam)
